det_01.label: Dataset provenance — 4 commercial rankings + OpenAlex neutral anchor
det_01.content: This is a multi-source theme dataset that aligns four commercial global university-ranking systems against a neutral, open research-output yardstick. THE (Times Higher Education, 2011-2016), ARWU/ShanghaiRanking (2005-2015) and CWUR (2012-2015) come from the widely-mirrored 'World University Rankings' compilation on GitHub (arnaudbenard/university-ranking, itself a copy of Myles O'Neill's classic Kaggle dataset). QS is the 2023 edition, mirrored from GeorgeM2000/QS-World-University-Ranking. The neutral anchor is OpenAlex, an open bibliometric index, fetched live from its REST API in June 2026 (top ~600 institutions by works_count). A normalised institution-name join produces a 189-institution five-way common core (THE2015 ∩ ARWU2015 ∩ CWUR2015 ∩ QS2023 ∩ OpenAlex); 2015 is the cleanest cross-system year, with QS (2023) and OpenAlex (current) attached as recent-state overlays. US News Best Global was the intended fourth 'big' system but has no clean downloadable CSV, so CWUR substitutes.

det_02.label: QS methodology — the reputation-survey pole
det_02.content: QS is the most reputation-driven of the four systems. In the pre-2024 methodology used for the 2023 edition in this dataset, Academic Reputation (a global survey of academics) was worth 40% and Employer Reputation (a survey of employers) 10% — so surveyed opinion alone drove HALF of a university's QS score. The remaining weight was split between Citations per Faculty (20%, research impact from Elsevier Scopus), Faculty/Student Ratio (20%, a teaching-capacity proxy) and international faculty + student share (5% each). Reputation responses are pooled over a rolling five-year window. This is why QS is the natural counter-pole to ARWU: its order is dominated by perception, not measured output.

sources.title: Understanding the Methodology: QS World University Rankings (TopUniversities)
facts: Academic Reputation 40%, Employer Reputation 10%, Citations per Faculty 20%, Faculty/Student Ratio 20%, International Faculty 5%, International Students 5% (pre-2024 methodology)
Citations-per-faculty data is drawn from Elsevier Scopus
The reputation surveys pool responses over the previous five years

det_03.label: THE methodology — reputation + citations blend
det_03.content: Times Higher Education blends performance and reputation. For the 2011-2023 editions (the family the 2011-2016 data here belongs to) THE used five pillars weighted Teaching 30%, Research 30%, Citations 30%, International outlook 7.5% and Industry income 2.5%. Reputation surveys are baked INSIDE the Teaching and Research pillars — 15% of the overall score from the teaching reputation survey plus 18% from the research reputation survey, i.e. about a third of the total is still surveyed opinion. But unlike QS, THE also gives fully 30% to field-normalised Citations (research influence), which is what lets citation-dense small institutions like Caltech top the table. THE later replaced this structure with 'WUR 3.0' in 2024.

sources.title: THE World University Rankings 2023: methodology
facts: Five pillars: Teaching 30%, Research 30%, Citations 30%, International outlook 7.5%, Industry income 2.5%
Reputation survey = 15% of the overall score inside Teaching and 18% inside Research (about 33% combined)

sources.title: Times Higher Education World University Rankings (Wikipedia)
facts: THE used its five-pillar methodology with Citations weighted ~30% from 2011 until the 2024 'WUR 3.0' overhaul

det_04.label: ARWU methodology — pure research & elite prizes
det_04.content: ARWU (the Shanghai Ranking), first published in 2003 by Shanghai Jiao Tong University and since 2009 by ShanghaiRanking Consultancy, is almost purely a research-and-prizes machine with NO reputation survey and NO teaching pillar. Its six indicators are: Alumni winning Nobel Prizes / Fields Medals (10%), Staff winning Nobel Prizes / Fields Medals (20%), Highly Cited Researchers per Clarivate (20%), papers in Nature & Science (20%), papers indexed in SCIE/SSCI (20%), and per-capita academic performance (10%). Because half the score rides on elite prizes and highly-cited-researcher counts, ARWU rewards a very different profile from QS — a university can sit top-5 in ARWU and middling in QS.

det_05.label: CWUR methodology — outcomes + research, no surveys
det_05.content: The Center for World University Rankings (CWUR) is distinctive because it uses NO reputation surveys and NO university-submitted data at all, relying only on independently verifiable indicators — which is exactly what makes it a useful 'commercial-but-not-survey-based' tiebreaker. Its current scheme groups seven indicators into four areas: Education 25% (alumni academic success relative to size), Employability 25% (alumni professional success), Faculty 10% (top academic distinctions) and Research 40% (output, high-quality publications, and influence/citations). Note: the 2012-2015 editions in THIS dataset use an OLDER eight-indicator version whose columns are RANKS (1 = best), not 0-100 scores — quality of education, alumni employment, quality of faculty, publications, influence, citations, broad impact and patents.

sources.title: Methodology | Center for World University Rankings
facts: CWUR uses no reputation surveys and no university data submissions, relying entirely on independently verifiable datasets
Current weighting: Education 25%, Employability 25%, Faculty 10%, Research 40% (output 10% + high-quality publications 10% + influence 10% + citations 10%)

det_06.label: OpenAlex — the neutral open research-output referee
det_06.content: OpenAlex is the story's neutral yardstick: a fully open, CC0 index of scholarly works, authors and institutions launched in January 2022 by the non-profit OurResearch as the successor to Microsoft Academic Graph (which Microsoft shut down at the end of 2021). It carries metadata for 200M+ works, is free via a high-volume REST API, and is positioned as an open alternative to the commercial Scopus and Web of Science databases the ranking companies rely on. For this story it supplies an order that owes nothing to any commercial methodology — raw works_count, total cited_by_count and h_index per institution. Its coverage is not perfectly even (documented discrepancies exist, e.g. for China), which the Analyst should treat as a caveat rather than a flaw.

det_07.label: BENCHMARK — how much each table is reputation vs measured output
det_07.content: The single most useful comparison for the Analyst is the reputation-vs-output weighting of each system, because it is the mechanical reason they disagree. Reputation-survey share of the total score: QS ~50% (Academic 40% + Employer 10%); THE ~33% (15% teaching survey + 18% research survey) but with a further 30% on citations; ARWU 0% (100% research output + elite prizes); CWUR 0% (surveys are excluded by design). OpenAlex is 0% reputation by construction — it is raw output/impact only. So along a 'perception ↔ measured output' axis the four systems fan out from QS (most perception) through THE to ARWU/CWUR (most output), with OpenAlex as the pure-output anchor beyond them.

det_08.label: The systems correlate weakly and crown different winners
det_08.content: Academic studies confirm the core premise: the big systems are statistically correlated but diverge sharply for individual universities and are unstable year to year. Reconciliation studies find pairwise rank correlations only in the 0.7-0.8 range for Times/QS/Shanghai, with 'many cases of high divergence and instability'. The disagreement even reaches the very top — in recent editions no single university leads all three (MIT tops QS, Oxford tops THE, Harvard tops ARWU), and this dataset's own years already disagree on #1 (ARWU 2015 and CWUR 2015 crown Harvard, THE 2015 crowns Caltech, QS 2023 crowns MIT). That the tables can't even agree who is best is the clearest evidence that 'best' is a weighting choice.

det_09.label: Why it matters — rankings steer real decisions
det_09.content: These tables are not academic parlour games; they move students, money and policy. In QS's own International Student Survey, roughly a quarter of prospective students (23.5%) said institutional ranking was the single most important factor in choosing a university and subject, and about a fifth (19.6%) said rankings shaped which COUNTRY they studied in. Ellen Hazelkorn's landmark work documents how rankings now reshape decisions not just for students and parents but for governments, funding agencies, employers and universities' own strategies — a 'global reputation race' in which a few weighting choices by three or four private companies ripple into national policy and billions in tuition and research funding. That stakes-per-decision is exactly why the disagreement between the tables is worth exposing.

det_10.label: Controversy — methodology changes cause artificial volatility
det_10.content: A university can jump or plunge dozens of places without changing at all, simply because a ranker changes its formula. QS's 2024 edition made what it called its largest-ever methodological change, adding three new indicators each worth 5% — International Research Network, Employment Outcomes and Sustainability — and rebalancing the surveys (Academic Reputation cut from 40% to 30%). Analysts noted this made year-on-year comparison essentially apples-to-oranges, and whole national systems moved (many Korean institutions fell under the new weights). This is a direct interpretive hook: the disagreement between systems is compounded by disagreement of each system WITH ITSELF over time, so a headline rank is a snapshot of a methodology, not a fixed truth.

det_11.label: Controversy — rankings can be gamed with bad data
det_11.content: Because several ranking indicators rely on self-reported institutional data, they can be manipulated. In 2022 Columbia University — ranked #2 by U.S. News — was found by its own mathematics professor Michael Thaddeus to have submitted inaccurate figures (class sizes, share of full-time faculty with terminal degrees, instructional spending). When corrected, Columbia fell from #2 to #18, one of the sharpest drops in the ranking's history; the university then withdrew from the undergraduate rankings and later reportedly settled related litigation for about $9 million. Although U.S. News is not one of the four systems in this dataset, the episode is the canonical warning that a headline rank is only as trustworthy as the data feeding it — reinforcing why an independent, non-submitted anchor like OpenAlex matters.

det_12.label: Controversy — top schools are boycotting the rankings
det_12.content: Institutions themselves increasingly reject the tables' authority. In 2023, led by Yale and Harvard law schools, dozens of top U.S. law schools and several medical schools boycotted the U.S. News rankings, refusing to supply data. Their objections go to methodology: Yale's dean argued the heavily weighted standardised-test metric penalises promising students who cannot afford test prep, Stanford's dean said the formula 'inappropriately discourages public service', and medical deans said the rankings 'measure the wrong things'. U.S. News responded by revising its formula to de-emphasise reputational surveys in favour of outcome measures. The revolt underscores the story's thesis: even the ranked elite dispute that a single weighting captures 'quality'.

det_13.label: Interpretive hook — the prestige loop and the size effect
det_13.content: Two mechanisms explain most of the disagreement and give the story its characters. First, reputation surveys create a self-reinforcing prestige (halo) loop that favours older, larger, English-speaking, already-famous universities — so QS's survey-heavy order rewards name recognition, which is partly downstream of past rankings. Second, normalisation choices flip the winners: THE and QS divide citations by faculty, so a tiny, citation-dense, science-focused school like Caltech can top THE, while a metric based on RAW output volume (OpenAlex works_count) instead crowns sprawling multi-faculty, medical-heavy giants like the University of Michigan or Toronto that no commercial table places first. The same universities therefore swing tens of places between systems purely because of what is weighted and whether it is size-normalised — Caltech (small, normalised winner) and Michigan (large, raw-volume winner) are the perfect two-sided illustration.

det_14.label: Scope note for the Analyst — caveats and confounds
det_14.content: Guidance for the analysis. (1) ERA MISMATCH is the dataset's main honest limitation: THE/ARWU/CWUR are 2015, QS is 2023, OpenAlex is current — so a strict 'they disagree' comparison is cleanest on the 2015 trio plus the anchor, treating QS and OpenAlex as recent-state overlays and flagging the mismatch explicitly. (2) The cross-system join is by NORMALISED INSTITUTION NAME (names differ across tables), which produced the 189-institution five-way core; a handful of edge cases may be mis-joined. (3) OpenAlex works_count REWARDS SIZE/AGE and medical output — big, old, hospital-affiliated universities dominate raw volume, so it is a yardstick of quantity, not quality; consider cited_by_count and h_index alongside it, and note that two_yr_mean_citedness has anomalous rows (e.g. Washington ~46 vs peers ~3-7) that look like data artefacts. (4) CWUR indicator columns are RANKS (1 = best), the OPPOSITE direction to the 0-100 scores in THE/ARWU/QS — do not mix them without inverting. (5) The QS 2023 edition uses the PRE-2024 legacy weights (Academic Reputation 40%), not the current formula.
